title: Language Acquisition
shortDescription: How readily you infer grammar and meaning from an unfamiliar constructed mini-language — a language-learning aptitude measure.
longDescription: Language Acquisition is built on the Artificial Grammar Learning (AGL) paradigm established by Arthur Reber (1967) — one of the foundational tasks in implicit-learning research. You're shown a set of "words" from an invented mini-language that all follow a hidden structural rule, without being told the rule. You then classify new, never-before-seen words as consistent or inconsistent with that same pattern. Performance reflects your ability to implicitly extract structure from exposure alone — a core mechanism behind natural language acquisition.
sourceNote: Uses an original finite-state grammar built for this assessment (letters B, F, G, K, S; a valid word is B, then zero or more FG/GF pairs, then K, then S) rather than Reber's exact 1967 grammar, which this platform can't verify reproducing correctly from memory without risking an inconsistent (and therefore incorrectly-scored) rule set — every example and test item below was hand-verified against this platform's own grammar definition. What's ported from Reber is the paradigm itself: implicit exposure to grammatical strings, then classification of novel strings as consistent or inconsistent with the pattern, without ever stating the rule outright.

sections.name: Word Classification
sections.description: Classifying novel words as following or breaking the pattern shown in the study examples.
sections.instructions: Study these words from an invented language called Velkarin. They all follow the same hidden pattern — don't try to work out the rule explicitly, just get a feel for what a Velkarin word looks like: BKS · BFGKS · BGFKS · BFGFGKS · BGFGFKS · BFGGFKS · BGFFGKS · BFGFGFGKS. For each word below, decide whether it follows the same pattern as those examples or breaks it.

scoringDimensions.label: Implicit Pattern Learning
scoringDimensions.description: Ability to extract and generalize structure from exposure alone, without explicit rule instruction.

resultRanges.title: Developing
resultRanges.description: Classifying novel words by "feel" after brief exposure is difficult right now — this implicit pattern-extraction skill responds well to more exposure, not conscious rule-hunting.
recommendations: Resist the urge to explicitly work out the rule — implicit learning tasks respond better to repeated exposure than analysis
Notice which specific letter combinations felt 'off' in words you got wrong — that intuition is the skill building
This paradigm mirrors early language exposure — the same mechanism that lets children absorb grammar without being taught rules

resultRanges.title: Average
resultRanges.description: Some sensitivity to the underlying pattern, but longer or more novel words still get misclassified.
recommendations: Re-read the study examples and let a 'shape' or 'rhythm' of the pattern form rather than counting letters
Trust your first instinct on borderline words — implicit learning is often more accurate than deliberate analysis

resultRanges.title: Strong
resultRanges.description: Reliable classification of novel words, including ones structurally different from the exact study examples.
recommendations: This is a strong implicit-learning signal — often correlated with picking up a new language's grammar quickly through immersion
Notice whether you can articulate any of the rule now, even partially — that's the implicit knowledge surfacing

resultRanges.title: Very Strong
resultRanges.description: Consistently accurate across both grammatical and ungrammatical novel words, generalizing well beyond the study set.
recommendations: This level of implicit pattern sensitivity is a genuine asset for immersion-based language learning
Try noticing patterns in real language input (song lyrics, headlines) the same intuitive way, without analyzing

resultRanges.title: Exceptional
resultRanges.description: Near-perfect classification of novel words — strong implicit extraction of structure from limited exposure.
recommendations: Consider how immersion-heavy learning methods (rather than rule-first instruction) might suit you especially well for a new language
This kind of statistical/structural learning also shows up in music and pattern-heavy domains — worth exploring there too
